claim: In the absence of external stimuli or overt behavior, the activity of the left and right cortical hemispheres shows fluctuations that are largely bilateral.
source: In the absence of external stimuli or overt behavior, the activity of the left and right cortical hemispheres shows fluctuations that are largely bilateral.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Bilateral fluctuations are largely responsible for the variability observed in cortical responses to sensory stimuli.
source: Here, we show that these fluctuations are largely responsible for the variability observed in cortical responses to sensory stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by the additive model results showing that bilateral fluctuations explain up to 60% of trial-by-trial variance.

claim: Bilateral fluctuations invested all cortical areas, particularly those closest to the midline.
source: Bilateral fluctuations invested all areas, particularly those closest to the midline.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing higher bilateral correlation in areas closer to the midline.

claim: Activity was less bilateral in the monocular region of primary visual cortex.
source: Activity was less bilateral in the monocular region of primary visual cortex and, especially during task engagement, in secondary motor cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D where V1m shows lower bilateral correlation than expected based on distance from midline.

claim: Activity was less bilateral in secondary motor cortex during task engagement.
source: Activity was less bilateral in the monocular region of primary visual cortex and, especially during task engagement, in secondary motor cortex.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1H showing significant reduction in M2 bilateral correlation during active task (p = 0.0013/0.013 before/after Bonferroni correction).

claim: Ongoing bilateral fluctuations dominated unilateral visual responses.
source: Ongoing bilateral fluctuations dominated unilateral visual responses, and interacted additively with them, explaining much of the variance in trial-by-trial activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the additive model results in Figure 7 showing bilateral fluctuations explain more variance than visual responses alone.

claim: Bilateral fluctuations interacted additively with visual responses.
source: Ongoing bilateral fluctuations dominated unilateral visual responses, and interacted additively with them, explaining much of the variance in trial-by-trial activity.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5 showing that bilateral ongoing activity changed offset but not scale parameters of contrast-response functions.

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity did not affect detection behavior.
source: Even though these fluctuations occurred in regions necessary for the task, they did not affect detection behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing no significant effect of bilateral activity on psychometric curves (p>0.05).

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity continues during visual stimulation.
source: We conclude that bilateral ongoing activity continues during visual stimulation and has a powerful additive impact on visual responses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4 where bilateral fluctuations persist after stimulus onset.

claim: Bilateral symmetry in ongoing activity has been documented in awake mice.
source: This bilateral symmetry has been documented both in awake mice (Mohajerani et al., 2010) and in awake humans (Fox et al., 2006; Tyszka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bilateral symmetry in ongoing activity has been documented in awake humans.
source: This bilateral symmetry has been documented both in awake mice (Mohajerani et al., 2010) and in awake humans (Fox et al., 2006; Tyszka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The degree of bilateral symmetry varies across cortical areas.
source: The degree of symmetry varies across cortical areas (Mohajerani et al., 2010), but the rules behind the differences across areas remain unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation and by the current study's data in Figure 2.

claim: Neural responses in primary visual cortex vary strongly from trial to trial even in response to an identical visual stimulus.
source: Even in response to an identical visual stimulus, neural responses in primary visual cortex are well-known to vary strongly from trial to trial (Tolhurst et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Trial-by-trial variability has been observed in spike trains.
source: This variability has been observed not only in the spike trains but also in intracellular recordings from single neurons (Anderson et al., 2000; Carandini, 2004) and in voltage imaging of neural populations (Arieli et al., 1996; Carandini et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trial-by-trial variability has been observed in intracellular recordings from single neurons.
source: This variability has been observed not only in the spike trains but also in intracellular recordings from single neurons (Anderson et al., 2000; Carandini, 2004) and in voltage imaging of neural populations (Arieli et al., 1996; Carandini et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trial-by-trial variability has been observed in voltage imaging of neural populations.
source: This variability has been observed not only in the spike trains but also in intracellular recordings from single neurons (Anderson et al., 2000; Carandini, 2004) and in voltage imaging of neural populations (Arieli et al., 1996; Carandini et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Widefield imaging allowed monitoring of bilateral ongoing activity and visually evoked response across hemispheres.
source: Widefield imaging allowed us to monitor bilateral ongoing activity and visually evoked response across hemispheres.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: Measurements were performed from mice expressing a voltage sensor and from mice expressing a calcium sensor.
source: To observe these forms of activity both in membrane potential and in spiking activity, we measured both from mice expressing a voltage sensor and from mice expressing a calcium sensor.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the experimental design described in Materials and methods.

claim: An additive model for the interaction of ongoing and evoked activities provided excellent fits to the data.
source: An additive model for the interaction of ongoing and evoked activities provided excellent fits to the data, explaining up to 60% of trial-by-trial variance in the observed imaging signal.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The additive model explained up to 60% of trial-by-trial variance in the observed imaging signal.
source: An additive model for the interaction of ongoing and evoked activities provided excellent fits to the data, explaining up to 60% of trial-by-trial variance in the observed imaging signal.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative results in Figure 7D showing 58 ± 3% variance explained in area PM.

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity did not seem to affect perceptual decisions.
source: On the other hand, bilateral ongoing activity did not seem to affect perceptual decisions, suggesting that it does not impact stimulus coding.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis in Figure 6 showing no significant effects on psychometric curves.

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity does not impact stimulus coding.
source: On the other hand, bilateral ongoing activity did not seem to affect perceptual decisions, suggesting that it does not impact stimulus coding.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of behavioral effects shown in Figure 6.

claim: During the pre-stimulus interval, strong bilateral voltage activity was observed over the entire dorsal cortex.
source: During the pre-stimulus interval, we observed strong bilateral voltage activity over the entire dorsal cortex (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Bilateral voltage activity involved multiple cortical areas.
source: This activity involved multiple cortical areas (Figure 1C) and was not accompanied by any obvious body movement (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and the associated video.

claim: Bilateral voltage activity was not accompanied by any obvious body movement.
source: This activity involved multiple cortical areas (Figure 1C) and was not accompanied by any obvious body movement (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Activity was largely symmetric between the left and right hemispheres.
source: As reported in previous studies (Mohajerani et al., 2010; Shimaoka et al., 2017), activity was largely symmetric between the left and right hemispheres.
evidence: This is supported by citations and by the current study's data in Figure 1.

claim: Symmetric, bilateral activity accounted for most of the power of the measured voltage signals at all measured frequencies.
source: Indeed, this symmetric, bilateral activity accounted for most of the power of the measured voltage signals, at all measured frequencies (Figure 1D): we did not observe significant difference in coherence across frequencies (2–7 Hz, p>0.05, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with statistical testing.

claim: There was no significant difference in coherence across frequencies (2–7 Hz) for voltage signals.
source: Indeed, this symmetric, bilateral activity accounted for most of the power of the measured voltage signals, at all measured frequencies (Figure 1D): we did not observe significant difference in coherence across frequencies (2–7 Hz, p>0.05, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-way ANOVA testing.

claim: Calcium signals reflect neuronal spiking.
source: These phenomena were not limited to voltage fluctuations, which might in principle be entirely subthreshold: they were also seen in calcium signals, which reflect neuronal spiking (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium imaging.

claim: Calcium activity during the pre-stimulus interval involved multiple cortical areas.
source: Calcium activity during the pre-stimulus interval involved multiple cortical areas and was also typically symmetric between the hemispheres (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and the associated video.

claim: Calcium activity during the pre-stimulus interval was typically symmetric between the hemispheres.
source: Calcium activity during the pre-stimulus interval involved multiple cortical areas and was also typically symmetric between the hemispheres (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and the associated video.

claim: Bilateral calcium activity accounted for most of the power of the measured calcium signals at all measured frequencies.
source: Just as with voltage signals, bilateral calcium activity accounted for most of the power of the measured calcium signals, and seemed to do so at all measured frequencies (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bilateral correlation was particularly strong in primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: This bilateral correlation was particularly strong in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and in medial visual areas such as PM (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Bilateral correlation was particularly strong in medial visual areas such as PM.
source: This bilateral correlation was particularly strong in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and in medial visual areas such as PM (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Bilateral correlation tended to decrease with a region's distance from the midline in mice expressing voltage indicators.
source: Bilateral correlation tended to decrease with a region's distance from the midline, both in mice-expressing voltage indicators (Figure 2C, pairwise correlation ρ = −0.44) and in mice-expressing calcium indicators (Figure 2D, pairwise correlation ρ = −0.42).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with quantitative correlation coefficient.

claim: Bilateral correlation tended to decrease with a region's distance from the midline in mice expressing calcium indicators.
source: Bilateral correlation tended to decrease with a region's distance from the midline, both in mice-expressing voltage indicators (Figure 2C, pairwise correlation ρ = −0.44) and in mice-expressing calcium indicators (Figure 2D, pairwise correlation ρ = −0.42).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with quantitative correlation coefficient.

claim: Correlation was lower than expected in the monocular region of primary visual cortex (V1m).
source: However, correlation was lower than expected in the monocular region of primary visual cortex, V1m and, when the animal was engaged in the task, in secondary motor cortex (M2, Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In area M2, low bilateral correlation may be related to task engagement.
source: In area M2, this low bilateral correlation may be related to task engagement, because bilateral correlation seemed to be higher when the animal was in a passive condition (Figure 2C,D, white circle).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D comparing active and passive conditions.

claim: The reduction in bilateral fluctuations seen with task engagement was specific to area M2.
source: Indeed, the reduction in bilateral fluctuations seen with task engagement was specific to area M2, where it was significant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical testing.

claim: In M2, there was a significant reduction in bilateral correlation during the active task (p = 0.0013/0.013 before/after Bonferroni correction, paired t test, n = 6 mice).
source: In M2, instead, there was a significant reduction during the active task (p = 0.0013/0.013 before/after Bonferroni correction, paired t test, n = 6 mice, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations continued following the onset of the visual stimulus.
source: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations continued following the onset of the visual stimulus and were typically larger than the unilateral visual responses (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations were typically larger than the unilateral visual responses.
source: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations continued following the onset of the visual stimulus and were typically larger than the unilateral visual responses (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Task stimuli elicited visual activity solely in contralateral cortex in area V1.
source: Task stimuli elicited visual activity solely in contralateral cortex, both in area V1 (Figure 4A, red traces) and in area PM (Figure 4B, red traces).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Task stimuli elicited visual activity solely in contralateral cortex in area PM.
source: Task stimuli elicited visual activity solely in contralateral cortex, both in area V1 (Figure 4A, red traces) and in area PM (Figure 4B, red traces).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The mean activity rose in the period 50–150 ms after stimulus onset.
source: The mean activity rose in the period 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, and increased with contrast as expected (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Mean activity increased with contrast as expected.
source: The mean activity rose in the period 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, and increased with contrast as expected (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E,F and is consistent with known properties of visual responses.

claim: The increase in mean activity was accompanied by an increase in standard deviation across trials.
source: Consistent with known variability of neural activity, this increase in mean was accompanied by an increase in standard deviation across trials (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: In the unstimulated hemisphere, the stimuli affected neither the mean activity nor the standard deviation of activity.
source: By contrast, in the unstimulated hemisphere, the stimuli affected neither the mean activity (Figure 4A,B, black traces) nor the standard deviation of activity (Figure 4C,D, black traces).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Bilateral fluctuations are not reduced by the onset of visual stimuli.
source: These results suggest that bilateral fluctuations are not reduced by the onset of visual stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that standard deviation in the unstimulated hemisphere does not change after stimulus onset.

claim: The offset parameter was significantly higher when ongoing activity was high (p = 0.0009, paired t test, n = 7 mice).
source: The offset parameter was significantly higher when ongoing activity was high (p = 0.0009, paired t test, n = 7 mice Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The scale parameter showed a mild increase when bilateral activity was high, but this increase was not significant (p>0.05, paired t test, n = 7 mice).
source: The scale parameter was much less affected: it appeared to show a mild increase when bilateral activity was high, but this increase was not significant (p>0.05, paired t test, n = 7 mice Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity changed offset but not scale in all visual areas.
source: This result held not only for PM but also for all other visual areas: bilateral ongoing activity changed offset but not scale (n = 7 in V1, n = 5 mice in AL, LM and RL, Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G,H across multiple visual areas.

claim: The effects of bilateral ongoing activity were due to fast changes in cortical activation, not to slow changes in cortical state.
source: Bilateral fluctuations are rapid and their effect is independent of arousal. These effects of bilateral ongoing activity were due to fast changes in cortical activation, not to slow changes in cortical state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 by analyzing synchronized vs. desynchronized states.

claim: The effects of bilateral ongoing activity were not related to slow changes in level of arousal.
source: Similarly, the effects of bilateral ongoing activity were not related to slow changes in level of arousal (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 by analyzing trials with different pupil diameters.

claim: The impact of bilateral ongoing activity could not be estimated through the typical procedure of measuring unilateral activity before stimulus onset.
source: Because ongoing activity changed rapidly and was largely bilateral, its impact could not be estimated through the typical procedure of measuring unilateral activity before stimulus onset (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 showing that prestimulus activity is less predictive than contralateral activity.

claim: The cross-correlation between corresponding regions on the two hemispheres typically decreased to 0 in ~100 ms.
source: Indeed, the cross-correlation between corresponding regions on the two hemispheres typically decreased to 0 in ~100 ms, and in some mice became negative afterwards (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations did not affect the behavior of the mouse in the task.
source: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations did not affect the behavior of the mouse in the task (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing no effect on psychometric curves.

claim: There was no effect of bilateral activity on the probability of choosing the correct side.
source: The two psychometric curves were essentially identical: there was no effect of bilateral activity on the probability of choosing the correct side (Figure 6A,C), or to choose a no-go response, which would be appropriate when stimulus is zero (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: There was no effect of bilateral activity on the probability to choose a no-go response.
source: The two psychometric curves were essentially identical: there was no effect of bilateral activity on the probability of choosing the correct side (Figure 6A,C), or to choose a no-go response, which would be appropriate when stimulus is zero (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Neither offset nor scale parameters of the perceptual contrast sensitivity function were significantly affected by bilateral ongoing activity (p>0.05, paired t test, n = 7 mice).
source: We fitted the behavioral responses with a simple probabilistic observer model (Burgess et al., 2017; Zatka-Haas et al., 2019), and measured offset and scale parameters of the perceptual contrast sensitivity function inferred by the model. Neither offset nor scale were significantly affected by bilateral ongoing activity (p>0.05, paired t test, n = 7 mice, Figure 6E,G).
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test shown in Figure 6E,G.

claim: The additive model explained 58 ± 3% of the variance in area PM (S.E. n = 7 mice).
source: In area PM, the additive model explained 58 ± 3% of the variance (S.E. n = 7 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the additive model analysis.

claim: The additive model accounted for up to 34% of trial-by-trial variability in the voltage signals for area PM.
source: For area PM, for instance, the additive model accounted for up to 34% of trial-by-trial variability in the voltage signals (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Much of the large variability observed across trials when performing widefield imaging experiments is not due to imaging noise, but rather to structured ongoing neural activity tightly coordinated across the hemispheres.
source: Much of the large variability observed across trials when performing widefield imaging experiments (Arieli et al., 1996; Carandini et al., 2015), therefore, is not due to imaging noise, but rather to structured ongoing neural activity tightly coordinated across the hemispheres.
evidence: This is inferred from the high variance explained by the bilateral component in the additive model.

claim: Voltage and calcium signals exhibited strong bilateral fluctuations in ongoing activity.
source: As reported previously (Mohajerani et al., 2010; Shimaoka et al., 2017; Vanni et al., 2017; Vanni and Murphy, 2014), voltage and calcium signals exhibited strong bilateral fluctuations in ongoing activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations and by the current study's data.

claim: The impact of bilateral fluctuations varied across cortical areas, and was stronger in areas closer to the midline.
source: In both types of signal, the impact of these bilateral fluctuations varied across cortical areas, and was stronger in areas closer to the midline.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Higher bilateral ongoing activity increased visual responses equally at all contrasts.
source: Higher bilateral ongoing activity increased visual responses equally at all contrasts, regardless of response amplitude, indicating that the interaction between ongoing activity and visually evoked responses was additive.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 where offset but not scale parameters changed.

claim: The interaction between ongoing activity and visually evoked responses was additive.
source: Higher bilateral ongoing activity increased visual responses equally at all contrasts, regardless of response amplitude, indicating that the interaction between ongoing activity and visually evoked responses was additive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the additive model results in Figure 5 and Figure 7.

claim: Bilateral ongoing fluctuations had a much larger effect on cortical activity than evoked visual responses.
source: A simple additive model provided good estimates of trial-by-trial visual response in all visual areas, and revealed that bilateral ongoing fluctuations had a much larger effect on cortical activity than evoked visual responses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D where bilateral component explains more variance than visual responses alone.

claim: The cortex exhibits clear bilateral activity during motor behavior.
source: The cortex exhibits clear bilateral activity during motor behavior (Musall et al., 2018), which is understandable given the symmetry involved in many body movements.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It is likely that bilateral fluctuations are at least partially mediated by callosal connections.
source: Regardless of their origin, it is likely that bilateral fluctuations are at least partially mediated by callosal connections.
evidence: This is inferred from anatomical knowledge and supported by subsequent discussion of callosal effects.

claim: The corpus callosum is the largest white matter tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres in placental mammalian brains.
source: Among these, the corpus callosum is the largest white matter tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres in placental mammalian brains.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Ongoing activity is less correlated across hemispheres in mutant mice that lack the corpus callosum.
source: Ongoing activity is less correlated across hemispheres in mutant mice that lack the corpus callosum (Mohajerani et al., 2010) and in rats after surgical section of the corpus callosum (Magnuson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ongoing activity is less correlated across hemispheres in rats after surgical section of the corpus callosum.
source: Ongoing activity is less correlated across hemispheres in mutant mice that lack the corpus callosum (Mohajerani et al., 2010) and in rats after surgical section of the corpus callosum (Magnuson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bilateral ongoing activity is reported in humans born without a corpus callosum.
source: However, ongoing bilateral activity is also reported in humans born without a corpus callosum (Tyszka et al., 2011), suggesting that bilateral fluctuations can also be sustained by other brain structures.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Bilateral fluctuations can be sustained by brain structures other than the corpus callosum.
source: However, ongoing bilateral activity is also reported in humans born without a corpus callosum (Tyszka et al., 2011), suggesting that bilateral fluctuations can also be sustained by other brain structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of bilateral activity in acallosal humans.

claim: Bilateral fluctuation represents shared activity across neurons, which impacts on response variability.
source: Bilateral fluctuation represents shared activity across neurons, which impacts on response variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the results showing bilateral fluctuations explain much of trial-by-trial variability.

claim: Ongoing activity is shared across large proportions of neurons and interacts additively with visually evoked responses.
source: Our widefield imaging result conforms to the previous electrophysiological report by Schölvinck et al. (2015), that ongoing activity is shared across large proportions of neurons and interacts additively with visually evoked responses, and that it accounts for a large fraction of trial-by-trial fluctuations in observed visually evoked activities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by current study's results.

claim: Ongoing activity accounts for a large fraction of trial-by-trial fluctuations in observed visually evoked activities.
source: Our widefield imaging result conforms to the previous electrophysiological report by Schölvinck et al. (2015), that ongoing activity is shared across large proportions of neurons and interacts additively with visually evoked responses, and that it accounts for a large fraction of trial-by-trial fluctuations in observed visually evoked activities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by current study's results.

claim: Global fluctuation is shared across hemispheres in an area-specific manner.
source: The present study extends this idea by demonstrating that such global fluctuation is actually shared across hemispheres, yet in an area-specific manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the area-specific patterns of bilateral correlation shown in Figure 2.

claim: A full understanding of activity in a population of neurons in one hemisphere may require recordings from the corresponding area of the other hemisphere.
source: Our results indicate that a full understanding of activity in a population of neurons in one hemisphere may require recordings from the corresponding area of the other hemisphere.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that contralateral activity is necessary to explain trial-by-trial variance.

claim: Activity in the prestimulus period had a smaller impact on evoked responses than simultaneously measured activity in the contralateral hemisphere.
source: Indeed, compared to bilateral activity, activity in the prestimulus period had a smaller impact on evoked responses than simultaneously measured activity in the contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ideal placement of a sensor in the contralateral hemisphere would be one that monitored the symmetrical populations to the ones of interest.
source: Given the specificity that we have observed in bilateral fluctuations, the ideal placement of a sensor in the contralateral hemisphere would be one that monitored the symmetrical populations to the ones of interest.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that bilateral fluctuations are area-specific (Figure 7C).

claim: A downstream readout mechanism may remove the bilateral fluctuations by taking the difference of activity on left and right visual cortices.
source: Perhaps, a downstream readout mechanism removes the bilateral fluctuations by taking the difference of activity on left and right visual cortices (Zatka-Haas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation and inferred from the lack of behavioral effects.

claim: It might be easy for the brain to ignore bilateral fluctuations during perceptual decisions based on vision.
source: It might thus be easy for the brain to ignore them during perceptual decisions based on vision, even though the fluctuations continue during visual stimulation and have a powerful additive impact on visual processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bilateral fluctuations do not affect behavior despite affecting neural responses.

claim: Mice were implanted with a head post and a thinned or intact skull cranial window over the dorsal part of both cortical hemispheres.
source: The nine mice (six males) were implanted with a head post and a thinned or intact skull cranial window (Drew et al., 2010) over the dorsal part of the both cortical hemispheres.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the surgical procedure.

claim: Imaging was conducted at 35 Hz in each purple and blue channel (70 Hz in total) for GCaMP imaging.
source: Imaging was conducted at 35 Hz in each purple and blue channel (70 Hz in total) with a nominal spatial resolution of 21.7 μm/pixel.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the imaging parameters.

claim: Imaging was conducted at 35 Hz in each blue and red/green channel (total 70 Hz) for VSFP imaging.
source: Imaging was conducted at 35 Hz in each blue and red/green channel (total 70 Hz), with a nominal spatial resolution of 21.7 μm/pixel.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the imaging parameters.

claim: Using 500 SVD components provided excellent fidelity in reconstructing the individual pixel traces.
source: Using 500 components provided excellent fidelity in reconstructing the individual pixel traces (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Filtering did not affect the ratio of unilateral to bilateral responses.
source: Finally, the signal was lowpass filtered with a cutoff of 7 Hz to attenuate signals from heartbeats. Filtering did not affect the ratio of unilateral to bilateral responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
